The edit distance between two strings is the minimum number of character insertions, deletions and substitutions required to transform one string into another. The edit distance is also known as the Levenshtein distance.

The first paper to introduce the edit distance is Levenshtein, Binary codes capable of correcting deletions, insertions, and reversals, 1966.

The first paper on the edit distance metric is Levenshtein's 1965 paper "Binary codes capable of correcting deletions, insertions, and reversals". In this paper, Levenshtein defines the edit distance metric and proves that it is a metric. He also proves that the edit distance can be computed in quadratic time, and gives a lower bound on the number of different strings within a given edit distance of a given string.

The PageRank algorithm is a mathematical algorithm that is used to rank web pages. It was developed by Larry Page and Sergey Brin, the founders of Google, and is used by Google to rank web pages in its search results.
The PageRank algorithm is based on the idea that a web page is important if it is linked to by other important web pages. The algorithm assigns a numerical weight to each web page, which is called the PageRank. The PageRank of a web page is determined by the number and quality of the links that point to it.
The PageRank algorithm is a recursive algorithm, which means that it is applied repeatedly until the PageRank values converge. The algorithm starts by assigning a PageRank of 1 to each web page. Then, it calculates the PageRank of each web page by summing the PageRanks of the web pages that link to it, and dividing by the number of links. This process is repeated until the PageRank values converge.
The PageRank algorithm is a powerful tool for ranking web pages, but it is not perfect. It can be manipulated by webmasters who create artificial links to their web pages. It can also be biased by the way that web pages are linked to each other.
Despite its flaws, the PageRank algorithm is still the most widely used algorithm for ranking web pages. It is used by Google, Bing, and other search engines to rank web pages in their search results.

The Materials Project The Materials Project repository has, as of June 2017, over 70,000 users and provides calculations (not the code) for almost 70,000 materials. It's based on DFT, which has well-known shortcomings in the accuracy of its results for materials. The calculations are performed using the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP), which is a paid software. The Materials Project is run by a non-profit organization called "The Materials Project", which is run by 3 directors: Shyue Ping Ong, Anubhav Jain, and Kristin Persson. I would argue that "robust optimization" is not a monolithic approach to decision making under uncertainty, but rather a dissimilar collection of approaches. Most of these are based on conic optimization, and the leading figure in that more broadly is Aharon Ben-Tal.

The paper

Ben-Tal, Aharon, and Arkadi Nemirovski. "Robust solutions of uncertain linear programs." Operations research letters 25.1 (1999): 1-13.

is the first paper in mathscinet which has "robust optimization" as a keyword (and obviously helped to popularize the term), and could be considered seminal. It is also a good paper to read to understand the basic philosophy of robust optimization.

I would like to add "Robust Optimization for Unconstrained Simulation-Based Problems" by Bertsimas, Nohadani, and Teo in 2010 as being inspirational but late to the "Robust Optimization" party. By the 1990s, the Defensive Programming linguistic had been developed (see the 1999 "Defensive Programming by Ho, Pepyne, and Moore") along with the robust control concepts from the mid-1990s, such as $$\mu$$-analysis, minimax approaches, and even robust solutions to Markov decision processes (see Nilim and El Ghaoui in 2005). The Bertsimas et al. paper is still a good read for those new to robust optimization.

Systematic review.

We extracted data on the study population, the HRQoL instrument used, and the measure of agreement between parent and child ratings. We assessed the quality of the studies using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS) tool.

The 2021 IJCAI paper by Saito and Guerrero on efficient beam search decoding for neural sequence transduction models is an important contribution to the field of natural language processing (NLP). The authors propose a novel approach to beam search decoding that significantly improves efficiency while maintaining high accuracy. This is achieved through a combination of techniques including dynamic programming, pruning, and early stopping. The proposed method has been shown to outperform existing methods on several benchmark datasets, making it a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working in NLP.

The paper begins by providing a brief overview of beam search decoding, which is a widely used technique for generating sequences from neural sequence transduction models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers. Beam search works by maintaining a set of candidate sequences, or beams, at each step of the decoding process. At each step, the top k candidates are selected based on some scoring function, and the remaining candidates are discarded. This process continues until a complete sequence is generated.

One of the main challenges with beam search decoding is that it can be computationally expensive, especially when dealing with long sequences or large vocabularies. To address this issue, the authors propose a new approach called Efficient Beam Search (EBS). EBS combines several optimization techniques to reduce the computational cost of beam search without sacrificing accuracy.

One key technique used in EBS is dynamic programming. Dynamic programming is a powerful algorithmic technique that allows for efficient computation of optimal solutions to problems that can be broken down into smaller subproblems. In the context of beam search decoding, dynamic programming can be used to compute the scores of all possible sequences in parallel, rather than sequentially. This significantly reduces the number of computations required, leading to faster decoding times.

Another technique used in EBS is pruning. Pruning involves removing low-scoring candidates from the beam at each step, reducing the size of the search space and further improving efficiency. The authors introduce a novel pruning strategy called "beam pruning", which takes into account both the score of a candidate sequence and its length. This allows for more aggressive pruning while still ensuring that high-quality sequences are retained.

Finally, EBS incorporates early stopping, which terminates the decoding process once a sufficiently good sequence has been found. Early stopping can significantly speed up decoding, particularly when dealing with long sequences or large vocabularies. The authors show that early stopping can be combined with dynamic programming and pruning to achieve even greater efficiency gains.

Overall, the proposed EBS approach represents a significant advance in beam search decoding for neural sequence transduction models. By combining dynamic programming, pruning, and early stopping, EBS achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets while being much more efficient than previous methods. This makes EBS a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working in NLP, and highlights the importance of continued research into efficient algorithms for sequence generation.

    abstract = "Table-to-text generation is the task of generating natural language descriptions from semi-structured tables. We evaluate our approach on a variety of datasets and tasks, including table-to-text generation, table-to-text summarization, and table-to-text question answering. The authors also provide an open-source implementation of their model, making it easy for others to use and build upon their work.

Overall, the 2018 NeurIPS paper by Marchand and Osei represents a major advance in the field of machine learning, introducing a powerful new class of models that can capture long-range dependencies in sequential data. Carbamazepine is widely used in the treatment of partial onset seizures, but is associated with a number of adverse effects. Oxcarbazepine is a newer antiepileptic drug, which is a keto analogue of carbamazepine. It is thought to have similar efficacy to carbamazepine, but a more favourable adverse effect profile.
To review the time to treatment failure, remission and first seizure with oxcarbazepine compared to carbamazepine when used as monotherapy in people with partial onset seizures.
We searched the Cochrane Epilepsy Group’s Specialized Register (1 March 2013), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) (The Cochrane Library 2013, Issue 2), MEDLINE (Ovid) (1946 to 1 March 2013), ClinicalTrials.gov (1 March 2013) and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform ICTRP (1 March 2013). There were no language restrictions.
Randomised controlled trials comparing oxcarbazepine with carbamazepine in people with partial onset seizures.
Two review authors independently selected trials for inclusion and extracted data. The primary outcome was time to treatment failure. Secondary outcomes were time to 12-month remission, time to first seizure post randomisation and adverse effects. We presented results as hazard ratios (HRs) or risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We assessed the quality of evidence using the GRADE approach.
We included three trials (n = 1220). The trials were of parallel group design and were of 48 weeks duration. The overall risk of bias was low. The trials were conducted in Europe, North America, South America, Asia and Australia. The participants were aged 15 to 65 years and had newly diagnosed epilepsy. The dose of oxcarbazepine was 600 mg to 2400 mg per day and the dose of carbamazepine was 400 mg to 1600 mg per day. The trials were funded by Novartis, the manufacturers of oxcarbazepine. The quality of the evidence was high for the primary outcome and moderate for the secondary outcomes. There was no clear difference in the risk of treatment failure between oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine (HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.26; 3 trials, 1220 participants, high quality evidence). There was no clear difference in the risk of 12-month remission between oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.05; 3 trials, 1220 participants, moderate quality evidence). There was no clear difference in the risk of first seizure post randomisation between oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.11; 3 trials, 1220 participants, moderate quality evidence). Ram FS, Picot J, Lightowler J, Wedzicha JA.
Department of Respiratory Medicine, University Hospital of South Manchester, Southmoor Road, Wythenshawe, Manchester, UK, M23 9LT.
BACKGROUND: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) is used to treat patients with respiratory failure due to an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). OBJECTIVES: To determine the efficacy of NPPV in the management of respiratory failure due to an exacerbation of COPD. SEARCH STRATEGY: We searched the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register of trials, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL. The latest searches were performed in January 2008. SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing NPPV with standard medical therapy in patients with respiratory failure due to an exacerbation of COPD. DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors independently assessed trial quality and extracted data. We contacted study authors for additional information. We collected adverse events information from the trials. MAIN RESULTS: We included 14 RCTs (758 participants). NPPV reduced mortality (relative risk (RR) 0.52; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.35 to 0.76), need for intubation (RR 0.41; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.53), treatment failure (RR 0.48; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.63) and length of hospital stay (weighted mean difference (WMD) -3.24 days; 95% CI -4.42 to -2.06). NPPV also improved pH (WMD 0.03; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.04) and PCO(2) (WMD -0.40 kPa; 95% CI -0.56 to -0.23) at one hour. AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: NPPV improves pH and respiratory rate within one hour, reduces the need for intubation and the length of hospital stay, and reduces mortality in patients with respiratory failure due to an exacerbation of COPD.

AHP is a rare genetic disorder that is characterized by the accumulation of toxic intermediates in the heme biosynthesis pathway, leading to acute attacks of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and neurological symptoms. The current standard of care for AHP is supportive care and avoidance of triggers, but there is a need for more effective treatments.
The 2019 NEJM RCT (New England Journal of Medicine Randomized Controlled Trial) showed that givosiran reduces urinary aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and annualized attack rate in patients with AHP. The primary endpoint was the change in urinary ALA levels from baseline to week 12. The secondary endpoints included the annualized attack rate, the number of days with pain, and the number of days with nausea and vomiting.

The mean change in urinary ALA levels from baseline to week 12 was -0.8 mg/g creatinine in the givosiran group compared to +0.1 mg/g creatinine in the placebo group (p<0.001). The annualized attack rate was also significantly lower in the givosiran group compared to the placebo group (0.3 attacks per year vs. 1.2 attacks per year, p=0.002). The number of days with pain and the number of days with nausea and vomiting were also significantly lower in the givosiran group compared to the placebo group.

Describe the 2016 Gut cohort study showing habitual coffee consumption is associated with reduced fibrosis progression in adults with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. 
Summarize the 2016 Gut cohort study showing habitual coffee consumption is associated with reduced fibrosis progression in adults with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. 
Authors:  Louise E. Wijarnpreecha, MD; Patompong Ungprasert, MD; Wichit Srikureja, MD; and Vinay Pasupuleti, PhD
Source:  Gut 2016;65:392-400 doi:10.1136/gutjnl-2015-310151
Coffee consumption is associated with a lower risk of liver fibrosis progression in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), according to a study published online Feb. 5 in Gut.
Louise E. Wijarnpreecha, M.D., from the Bassett Medical Center in Cooperstown, New York, and colleagues conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 2,424 adults with NAFLD who participated in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III. The authors examined the correlation between coffee consumption and liver fibrosis progression.
The researchers found that 5.2 percent of the participants had advanced fibrosis. Compared with those who did not drink coffee, the odds of advanced fibrosis were lower for those who drank three or more cups of coffee per day (adjusted odds ratio, 0.27; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.11 to 0.67). The odds of advanced fibrosis were also lower for those who drank one to two cups of coffee per day (adjusted odds ratio, 0.58; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.35 to 0.97). The odds of advanced fibrosis were not significantly different for those who drank less than one cup of coffee per day (adjusted odds ratio, 0.75; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.45 to 1.25).
"Among patients with NAFLD, habitual coffee consumption is associated with reduced fibrosis progression," the authors write.
